options.a: Complete, accurate, timely submission with no missing info
options.b: Accepted by the clearinghouse, even if payer edits flag errors
options.c: Paid in full at the billed charge on first submission
options.d: Submitted within 12 months even if the NPI is missing

distractorExplanations.b: Clearinghouse acceptance only passes format edits; a clean claim must also pass payer edits without needing more information.
distractorExplanations.c: Clean means processable without extra information; payment is made at the allowed amount, not the billed charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Meeting the 12-month filing limit does not make a claim clean when a required identifier like the NPI is missing.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Clean claims contain all data needed for adjudication without additional information. Required identifiers such as the NPI must be present.

options.a: Institutional inpatient and outpatient hospital services
options.b: Professional physician/outpatient services
options.c: Dental procedures coded with CDT codes
options.d: Retail pharmacy prescription claims

distractorExplanations.a: Institutional hospital services are billed on the UB-04 (CMS-1450), not the professional CMS-1500.
distractorExplanations.c: Dental procedures with CDT codes are billed on the ADA dental claim form, not the CMS-1500.
distractorExplanations.d: Retail pharmacy claims use the NCPDP standard, not the CMS-1500 professional claim form.

options.a: Appealed in writing to the payer with supporting records
options.b: Billed to the patient as self-pay until coverage is confirmed
options.c: Resubmitted as a corrected claim with frequency code 7
options.d: Corrected with verified insurance information and resubmitted

distractorExplanations.a: Appeals are for adjudicated denials; a clearinghouse rejection never reached adjudication, so it is corrected and resubmitted.
distractorExplanations.b: The subscriber ID should be verified and corrected first; shifting the bill to the patient skips a fixable data error.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequency code 7 replaces a claim the payer already adjudicated; a rejected claim was never accepted and goes as a new claim.

options.a: Primary and secondary coverage; primary pays first per rules
options.b: One plan with a deductible and coinsurance split
options.c: A liability claim where the payer recovers from a third party
options.d: Coverage that ended, requiring retroactive eligibility review

distractorExplanations.b: Deductible and coinsurance are cost sharing within a single plan; COB requires two or more plans covering the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Recovering costs from a liable third party is subrogation, not coordination of benefits between two plans.
distractorExplanations.d: A terminated policy is an eligibility issue; COB applies only when more than one active plan covers the patient.

options.a: Claim lacked a prior authorization number for the service
options.b: Claim submitted after payer deadline without valid exception
options.c: Claim matched one already processed for the same date of service
options.d: Claim listed a diagnosis that does not support medical necessity

distractorExplanations.a: A missing authorization number triggers a prior authorization denial, not a timely filing denial.
distractorExplanations.c: Matching a previously processed claim triggers a duplicate claim denial, not a timely filing denial.
distractorExplanations.d: A diagnosis that fails to support the service triggers a medical necessity denial, not a filing-deadline denial.

options.a: A commercial plan may deny a service the patient still wants
options.b: Medicare statutorily excludes the service, so a notice is required
options.c: Medicare may not pay for service and patient chooses to proceed
options.d: Medicare will deny a claim because the provider coded it incorrectly

distractorExplanations.a: The ABN is a Medicare fee-for-service form; commercial plans use their own patient waiver or financial agreement.
distractorExplanations.b: An ABN is not required for statutorily excluded services such as routine dental; it may be issued only voluntarily.
distractorExplanations.d: Coding errors are corrected by the provider; an ABN cannot shift liability for the provider's own billing mistakes.

options.a: Request for additional records to support a pending claim
options.b: Status of a submitted claim in the payer's processing queue
options.c: Patient eligibility and benefit details for a date of service
options.d: Explanation of payment, adjustments, and reason codes

distractorExplanations.a: Requests for supporting records are additional documentation requests or claim attachments, not the 835 remittance.
distractorExplanations.b: Claim status inquiries and responses use the 276/277 transactions, not the 835 remittance advice.
distractorExplanations.c: Eligibility and benefit details come from the 270/271 transactions, not the 835 remittance advice.

options.a: Same service billed twice with same date/provider without modifier
options.b: Two related procedures billed together that NCCI bundles
options.c: A corrected claim sent with frequency code 7 to replace the original
options.d: A repeat procedure billed with modifier 76 on the same day

distractorExplanations.b: Billing two bundled procedures triggers an NCCI procedure-to-procedure edit, not a duplicate claim denial.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequency code 7 tells the payer the claim replaces the original, which is how duplicate denials are avoided.
distractorExplanations.d: Modifier 76 identifies a repeat procedure by the same physician, which prevents a duplicate denial rather than causing it.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Payers detect duplicate service lines; use frequency/modifier for corrections/voids. A resubmission indicator (claim frequency code) also prevents duplicate denials.

options.a: Pre-op visit a week before surgery, surgery, and all follow-up for one year
options.b: Pre-op visit day before major surgery, surgery, and follow-up within global period
options.c: Surgery and follow-up, plus treatment of a new unrelated problem afterward
options.d: Surgery itself, with routine post-op visits billed separately with modifier 24

distractorExplanations.a: For major surgery the global includes pre-op visits from the day before and 90 days of follow-up, not a week before and a year after.
distractorExplanations.c: An unrelated problem treated during the global period is billed separately with modifier 24, not included in the package.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine post-op visits are included in the global package; modifier 24 is for unrelated E/M services.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Global periods bundle certain pre/post op services; separate billing rules apply. Global package contents follow CPT and payer rules.

options.a: Frequency code 7 void then new claim or frequency 8 replacement
options.b: Frequency code 1 resubmission of the same claim with the changes
options.c: A written appeal asking the payer to edit the original claim
options.d: Frequency code 8 void then new claim or frequency 7 replacement

distractorExplanations.a: This swaps the codes: frequency 8 voids a prior claim and frequency 7 replaces it.
distractorExplanations.b: Frequency code 1 marks an original claim, so resending a paid claim with code 1 causes a duplicate denial.
distractorExplanations.c: Appeals contest the payer's adjudication decision; the provider's own errors are fixed with a corrected or voided claim.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Electronic claims use frequency/type codes to void or replace prior submission. Which route to use follows each payer's rules.

options.a: Service detail, insurance payments/adjustments, patient responsibility
options.b: Total billed charges as the balance due, before any insurance adjustments
options.c: Service detail and the full allowed amount owed by the patient
options.d: Diagnosis codes and clinical notes justifying each service billed

distractorExplanations.b: Contractual adjustments and insurance payments must be applied; billing the full charge overstates what the patient owes.
distractorExplanations.c: The patient owes only the cost share left after the plan's payment, not the full allowed amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Patient statements are financial documents; clinical notes are not included and would add needless PHI exposure.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Statements reflect allowed amounts, payments, adjustments, and remaining patient liability. The balance shown should align with the EOB.

options.a: Patient's group health plan as primary, with WC billed as secondary
options.b: WC payer info, injury date, employer, and diagnosis linked to work injury
options.c: Medicare as primary payer with the employer listed as secondary
options.d: Patient copay collected at check-in, with the balance billed to the employer

distractorExplanations.a: For a work injury the workers' compensation carrier is primary; the group health plan is not billed first.
distractorExplanations.c: Under Medicare Secondary Payer rules, workers' compensation is primary for a work injury and Medicare is not.
distractorExplanations.d: WC patients generally owe no copay, and the claim goes to the WC carrier, not directly to the employer.

options.a: Left as is, since underbilling causes no compliance exposure
options.b: Offset by billing a higher-level code on future claims
options.c: Corrected through rebilling/contract review and internal audit
options.d: Reported to the OIG as a potential false claim violation

distractorExplanations.a: Inaccurate claims in either direction are a compliance issue; repeated underbilling signals a process error to correct.
distractorExplanations.b: Billing a higher code than documented to make up lost revenue is upcoding, which is fraud.
distractorExplanations.d: Accidental underbilling causes no overpayment to report; it is corrected internally through rebilling and audit.

options.a: Procedures and services performed by physicians
options.b: Supplies, drugs, and durable medical equipment
options.c: Inpatient hospital procedures performed
options.d: Diagnoses, symptoms, and reasons for encounter

distractorExplanations.a: Physician procedures and services are reported with CPT codes, not ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes.
distractorExplanations.b: Supplies, drugs, and DME are reported with HCPCS Level II codes, not ICD-10-CM.
distractorExplanations.c: Inpatient hospital procedures are coded with ICD-10-PCS, a separate system from ICD-10-CM.

options.a: Established patient office visit level 3
options.b: New patient office visit level 3
options.c: Established patient office visit level 4
options.d: Office consultation, level 3

distractorExplanations.b: A new patient level 3 office visit is CPT 99203; 99213 is the established patient code.
distractorExplanations.c: An established patient level 4 office visit is CPT 99214, one level above 99213.
distractorExplanations.d: Office consultations use the 99242-99245 range (such as 99243), not 99213.

options.a: Distinct procedural service on the same day as another procedure
options.b: Significant, separately identifiable E/M on same day as procedure
options.c: Unrelated E/M by the same physician during a postoperative period
options.d: Decision for major surgery made at the E/M the day before or day of

distractorExplanations.a: A distinct procedure on the same day is reported with modifier 59 (or an X modifier), not modifier 25.
distractorExplanations.c: An unrelated E/M during a postoperative global period uses modifier 24, not modifier 25.
distractorExplanations.d: The decision for major surgery at an E/M the day before or day of surgery uses modifier 57.

options.a: Billing component codes separately instead of one bundled code
options.b: Billing a lower level than documented to avoid an audit
options.c: Billing higher level service than documented/supported
options.d: Billing for a service that was not actually performed

distractorExplanations.a: Billing components separately instead of the comprehensive code is unbundling, not upcoding.
distractorExplanations.b: Billing below the documented level is downcoding (undercoding), the opposite of upcoding.
distractorExplanations.d: Billing for services never rendered is phantom billing, a separate fraud from inflating the service level.

options.a: Service ordered by a licensed provider and requested by the patient
options.b: Service listed as a covered benefit in the patient's insurance plan
options.c: Service supported by a signed ABN from the patient before treatment
options.d: Service reasonable and necessary for diagnosis/treatment

distractorExplanations.a: An order plus patient preference does not establish necessity; the diagnosis and record must justify the service.
distractorExplanations.b: A covered benefit can still be denied as not medically necessary for this patient's diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.c: An ABN shifts financial liability to the patient; it does not establish medical necessity.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Payers deny services not justified by diagnosis and clinical documentation. Medical necessity must be supported in the medical record.

options.a: Supplies, drugs, ambulance, and DME not in CPT
options.b: Physician procedures and E/M services in CPT
options.c: Inpatient procedures in the ICD-10-PCS code set
options.d: Category III emerging technology codes

distractorExplanations.b: Physician procedures and E/M services are CPT codes, which are HCPCS Level I, not Level II.
distractorExplanations.c: Inpatient procedures are coded in ICD-10-PCS, a separate system from HCPCS Level II.
distractorExplanations.d: Category III codes for emerging technology are part of CPT, not HCPCS Level II.

options.a: Default to the right side when the note does not specify
options.b: Match clinical documentation specifying side when applicable
options.c: Be coded as bilateral whenever both sides were examined
options.d: Be taken from the order or referral rather than the provider's note

distractorExplanations.a: Defaulting to a side is guessing; when laterality is undocumented, query the provider or use the unspecified code.
distractorExplanations.c: Bilateral codes apply only when the condition affects both sides, not when both sides were merely examined.
distractorExplanations.d: Code assignment follows the treating provider's documentation of the encounter, not the order or referral.

options.a: Billing a higher E/M level than the provider's documentation supports
options.b: Claims for services lacking a covered diagnosis under a local coverage determination
options.c: Improper unbundling of component codes billed separately when bundled
options.d: Claims submitted after the payer's timely filing deadline

distractorExplanations.a: Upcoding E/M levels is found through documentation review, not NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits.
distractorExplanations.b: Diagnosis coverage checks come from LCD/NCD medical necessity edits, not NCCI bundling edits.
distractorExplanations.d: Late claims are stopped by timely filing rules, not by NCCI coding edits.

options.a: Condition that consumed the most resources during the hospital stay
options.b: Condition listed first by the physician on the admission order
options.c: Most serious condition treated during the stay, even if not the reason
options.d: Condition established after study to be chiefly responsible for admission

distractorExplanations.a: Resource use does not define the principal diagnosis; it is the condition found after study to cause the admission.
distractorExplanations.b: The admitting diagnosis on the order may change after study; the principal diagnosis is set after study.
distractorExplanations.c: Severity does not decide it; a serious condition that did not cause the admission is a secondary diagnosis.

options.a: Medical decision making and/or total time on date of encounter
options.b: History, exam, and medical decision making as the three key components
options.c: Total time including staff time spent on the days before the visit
options.d: Number of body systems examined and documented in the note

distractorExplanations.b: History, exam, and MDM as three key components were the 1995/1997 rules replaced for office visits in 2021.
distractorExplanations.c: Time-based leveling counts only physician or QHP time on the date of the encounter, not staff time or other days.
distractorExplanations.d: Since 2021 the exam is performed as medically appropriate and no longer drives the office E/M level.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: E/M levels based on MDM elements or time per current CMS/AMA guidelines. The level must be supported by documentation.

options.a: Nature of the injury, such as a fracture or open wound
options.b: Mechanism/circumstance of injury or poisoning when documented
options.c: Patient status factors such as a history of injury
options.d: Sequelae of an injury, identified by the 7th character S

distractorExplanations.a: The nature of the injury is coded with Chapter 19 S and T codes; external cause codes add how it happened.
distractorExplanations.c: Status and history factors are captured with Z codes, not external cause codes.
distractorExplanations.d: Sequelae are shown by the 7th character S on the injury code itself, not by an external cause code.

options.a: Modifier 22 to show the service was more complex than usual
options.b: A Category III code reported alongside it for tracking
options.c: Description and often comparable code with documentation
options.d: The closest listed code billed with modifier 52 attached

distractorExplanations.a: Modifier 22 reports increased work on an existing listed code; it does not apply to unlisted codes.
distractorExplanations.b: When a Category III code exists it is reported instead of an unlisted code, not alongside it.
distractorExplanations.d: Modifier 52 reports a reduced service; substituting a listed code for a different service misrepresents what was done.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Unlisted codes need report/comparison to establish value and medical necessity. The documentation must support the unique service.

options.a: Repeat procedure by the same physician on the same day
options.b: Significant, separately identifiable E/M on a procedure day
options.c: Bilateral procedure performed on both sides at the same operative session
options.d: Distinct procedural service when no more specific modifier applies

distractorExplanations.a: A repeat procedure by the same physician is reported with modifier 76, not modifier 59.
distractorExplanations.b: A separate E/M on a procedure day is reported with modifier 25, not modifier 59.
distractorExplanations.c: A bilateral procedure at the same session is reported with modifier 50, not modifier 59.

options.a: Conflicts or lacks specificity needed for accurate code assignment
options.b: Supports a higher-paying code that the provider did not document anywhere
options.c: Is complete but the coder prefers a more common code
options.d: Is signed by a resident rather than the attending physician

distractorExplanations.b: Queries must be non-leading; prompting for a higher-paying code the provider did not document is noncompliant.
distractorExplanations.c: Complete, clear documentation needs no query; coder preference never justifies changing what is documented.
distractorExplanations.d: Resident signatures raise attestation rules, not the clinical-clarity issue a coding query resolves.

options.a: Claims require SNOMED CT codes; ICD-10-CM is used for clinical problem lists
options.b: Claims require ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes; SNOMED supports clinical documentation
options.c: SNOMED CT replaces CPT for procedures on the CMS-1500 claim form
options.d: SNOMED CT codes map one-to-one to ICD-10-CM, so either can be billed

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the roles: claims require ICD-10-CM, while SNOMED CT supports clinical documentation in the EHR.
distractorExplanations.c: Procedures on the CMS-1500 are still reported with CPT/HCPCS; SNOMED CT is not a billing code set.
distractorExplanations.d: SNOMED-to-ICD mapping is not one-to-one, and payers accept only ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes on claims.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: SNOMED CT is clinical terminology; billing uses ICD-10-CM mapped from documentation. SNOMED CT terms are mapped to ICD-10-CM for billing.

options.a: Physician services, outpatient care, DME, and preventive services
options.b: Inpatient hospital, long-term custodial nursing care, and routine dental
options.c: Inpatient hospital, skilled nursing (limited), hospice, some home health
options.d: Private plan bundling hospital, medical, and usually drug coverage

distractorExplanations.a: Physician services, outpatient care, DME, and preventive services are Medicare Part B, not Part A.
distractorExplanations.b: Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care or routine dental under Part A.
distractorExplanations.d: A private plan bundling hospital, medical, and drug coverage is Medicare Advantage (Part C).

options.a: Inpatient hospital, skilled nursing, hospice, and some home health
options.b: Outpatient prescription drugs through private stand-alone plans
options.c: Long-term custodial nursing home care and routine hearing aids
options.d: Physician services, outpatient care, DME, preventive services

distractorExplanations.a: Inpatient hospital, skilled nursing, and hospice are Medicare Part A benefits, not Part B.
distractorExplanations.b: Outpatient prescription drugs through stand-alone private plans are Medicare Part D.
distractorExplanations.c: Original Medicare does not cover custodial nursing home care or routine hearing aids under Part B.

options.a: Federal CMS rules that apply identically in every state
options.b: State rules, managed care plans, and fee schedules
options.c: The patient's Medicare Part B enrollment status alone
options.d: The provider's commercial contract rates and network tier

distractorExplanations.a: Medicaid is administered by each state within federal guidelines, so rules differ from state to state.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicaid eligibility rests on state income and category rules; Medicare enrollment only matters for dual eligibles.
distractorExplanations.d: Commercial contract rates do not set Medicaid billing; state fee schedules and Medicaid managed care plans do.

options.a: Veterans receiving care at VA medical centers
options.b: Dependents of veterans with service-connected disability
options.c: Uniformed service members, retirees, and families
options.d: Federal civilian employees and their dependents

distractorExplanations.a: Care at VA medical centers is VA health care, a separate system from TRICARE.
distractorExplanations.b: Dependents of certain permanently disabled veterans are covered by CHAMPVA, not TRICARE.
distractorExplanations.d: Federal civilian employees are covered through the FEHB program, not TRICARE.

options.a: Perform the MRI and bill the patient's secondary plan instead
options.b: Perform the MRI and appeal after the claim is denied for no auth
options.c: Schedule the MRI once the patient signs a Medicare ABN
options.d: Review denial reason, peer-to-peer if available, patient notification

distractorExplanations.a: The secondary plan follows the primary's determination; billing it does not cure a missing primary authorization.
distractorExplanations.b: Proceeding without authorization risks nonpayment; the denial reason and peer-to-peer review come before service.
distractorExplanations.c: The ABN is a Medicare fee-for-service notice and does not apply to a commercial payer's denial.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Appeals and peer review may overturn; patient informed of options and liability. An alternative plan of care may also be discussed.

options.a: Group health plan due to active employment over certain size/age rules
options.b: Patient has a Medigap supplement policy purchased through a private insurer
options.c: Patient is 65+ and covered by a retiree group health plan
options.d: Patient is enrolled in Medicaid as well as Medicare Part B

distractorExplanations.b: Medigap pays after Medicare; it is a supplement, not a primary payer under MSP rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Retiree coverage is not based on current employment, so it pays secondary to Medicare.
distractorExplanations.d: Medicaid is the payer of last resort, so Medicare stays primary for dual-eligible patients.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: MSP provisions determine when Medicare pays secondary to other insurance. Other situations where other insurance is primary, such as liability or WC, also apply.

options.a: Receives a discounted fee for each service billed to the plan
options.b: Receives fixed per-member payment and manages care within budget
options.c: Receives a fixed payment per admission based on the DRG
options.d: Receives a bonus based on quality scores in addition to fees

distractorExplanations.a: A discounted fee per service is discounted fee-for-service, not capitation.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed payment per admission by DRG is a case rate, not a per-member capitated payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Quality bonuses on top of fees describe pay-for-performance, not a fixed per-member capitation.

options.a: The provider's bill for the remaining balance after insurance
options.b: The payer's decision on a prior authorization request
options.c: What provider billed, allowed amount, plan paid, patient owes
options.d: The provider's detailed payment remittance and CARC codes

distractorExplanations.a: The provider's bill for the remaining balance is the patient statement, which follows the EOB.
distractorExplanations.b: Prior authorization decisions come in a separate determination letter, not the EOB.
distractorExplanations.d: Remittance detail with CARC codes goes to the provider on the ERA/RA, not to the patient as an EOB.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: EOB explains adjudication; provider statement may follow for patient balance. It is usually not a bill itself.

options.a: Denied unless the member obtained prior authorization
options.b: Covered only at the out-of-network benefit level and cost share
options.c: Paid by the home state's Medicaid program instead of Blue Cross
options.d: Processed under emergency/urgent rules per member contract

distractorExplanations.a: The ACA bars plans from requiring prior authorization for emergency services.
distractorExplanations.b: Federal rules require in-network cost sharing for emergency care, even out of network.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicaid does not pick up claims for a commercially insured Blue Cross member's emergency care.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Emergency services have special network/payment rules under ACA and plan terms. Federal protections such as the ACA and No Surprises Act also apply.

options.a: Prescription drug coverage through private plans
options.b: Inpatient hospital and hospice coverage
options.c: Private plans bundling Parts A and B into one product
options.d: Physician and outpatient services coverage

distractorExplanations.b: Inpatient hospital and hospice coverage is Medicare Part A, not Part D.
distractorExplanations.c: Private plans bundling Parts A and B are Medicare Advantage (Part C), not Part D.
distractorExplanations.d: Physician and outpatient services are Medicare Part B, not Part D.

options.a: The Social Security Administration's regional Medicare office
options.b: Palmetto GBA under special Medicare rules for railroad beneficiaries
options.c: The local A/B MAC that handles other Medicare claims in the state
options.d: The Railroad Retirement Board claims unit in Chicago directly

distractorExplanations.a: SSA handles enrollment for many beneficiaries but does not process Medicare claims.
distractorExplanations.c: Railroad Medicare Part B claims go to the RRB Specialty MAC, not the local A/B MAC.
distractorExplanations.d: The RRB handles enrollment and entitlement; claims are processed by its contracted Specialty MAC.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Railroad Retirement Board beneficiaries have Medicare processed through designated contractors. Palmetto GBA is the Railroad Retirement Board Specialty MAC.

options.a: An insurance carrier that bears the claim risk
options.b: The state insurance department's claims fund
options.c: Employer/plan administrator often using TPA
options.d: The stop-loss carrier on every claim submitted

distractorExplanations.a: A carrier bearing the claim risk describes a fully insured plan, not a self-funded one.
distractorExplanations.b: Self-funded ERISA plans are not state-insured; no state fund pays their claims.
distractorExplanations.d: Stop-loss reimburses the employer only above set thresholds; it does not pay each claim.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Self-funded ERISA plans use administrator; billing follows plan documents. The employer, not a fully insured carrier, bears the claim risk.

options.a: Specialist visits covered at higher cost share without a referral
options.b: Referral needed only for out-of-network specialists
options.c: Referral needed for every visit, including emergency department care
options.d: PCP referral/authorization needed for specialist except emergencies

distractorExplanations.a: Self-referral to specialists at higher cost sharing describes a PPO, not an HMO.
distractorExplanations.b: Requiring referrals mainly for out-of-network care resembles a POS plan; HMOs need referrals in network too.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency care is exempt from referral requirements under HMO plans and federal rules.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: HMOs gatekeep specialty care through PCP/referrals and network. Exact referral rules follow each plan.

options.a: Before service when possible and at intervals for ongoing treatment
options.b: At the first visit only, since coverage rarely changes during the year
options.c: After claim denial, to confirm the reason for the payer's decision
options.d: At each annual plan renewal, unless the patient reports a change

distractorExplanations.b: Coverage can change at any time through job loss or plan changes, so one check at the first visit is not enough.
distractorExplanations.c: Checking eligibility after a denial is too late; verification before service prevents the denial.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for renewal or a patient report misses mid-year terminations; verify before each service when possible.

options.a: Administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic PHI
options.b: Safeguarding PHI, minimum necessary use/disclosure, patient rights
options.c: Patient written consent before any PHI is used for treatment
options.d: Notification to patients within 60 days of any PHI breach

distractorExplanations.a: Administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for ePHI are HIPAA Security Rule requirements, not the Privacy Rule.
distractorExplanations.c: The Privacy Rule permits use of PHI for treatment, payment, and operations without written authorization.
distractorExplanations.d: Breach notification is the separate Breach Notification Rule and applies to unsecured PHI breaches.

options.a: Billing errors caught and refunded within 60 days of identification
options.b: Honest coding mistakes made without reckless disregard
options.c: Knowingly submitting false claims for government payment
options.d: Submitting false claims to a commercial insurer only

distractorExplanations.a: Returning an identified overpayment within 60 days is how providers avoid False Claims Act liability.
distractorExplanations.b: FCA liability requires knowledge, including deliberate ignorance or reckless disregard; honest mistakes are not enough.
distractorExplanations.d: The federal FCA covers claims paid with government funds; purely commercial fraud falls under other laws.

options.a: Written policies, a compliance officer, and annual external accreditation
options.b: Training, auditing, and mandatory self-disclosure of every error to CMS
options.c: Written policies, training, and incentive pay tied to billing volume
options.d: Written policies, training, auditing, enforcement, and response procedures

distractorExplanations.a: External accreditation is not one of the seven OIG compliance program elements.
distractorExplanations.b: Overpayments are reported and returned, but OIG does not require self-disclosing every billing error to CMS.
distractorExplanations.c: Incentive pay tied to billing volume creates fraud risk; it is not an OIG compliance element.

options.a: Physician self-referral for designated health services absent exception
options.b: Offering anything of value to induce referrals of federal program patients
options.c: Referring patients for any service to an entity the physician owns
options.d: Submitting claims the provider knows to be false to Medicare

distractorExplanations.b: Remuneration to induce federal program referrals is the Anti-Kickback Statute, not the Stark Law.
distractorExplanations.c: Stark covers only designated health services, and exceptions exist; it does not bar referrals for every service.
distractorExplanations.d: Knowingly submitting false claims is the False Claims Act, not the Stark self-referral law.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Stark restricts DHS referrals where physician has financial relationship unless exception met. It applies when the physician or an immediate family member has a financial relationship with the entity.

options.a: Physician referrals for DHS to entities with a financial relationship
options.b: Remuneration to induce referrals for services paid by federal programs
options.c: Knowingly submitting false claims to Medicare or Medicaid
options.d: Billing for services furnished by an excluded individual

distractorExplanations.a: Physician referrals for designated health services to financially related entities fall under the Stark Law.
distractorExplanations.c: Knowingly submitting false claims is governed by the False Claims Act, not the Anti-Kickback Statute.
distractorExplanations.d: Billing for services by an excluded person triggers OIG exclusion penalties (CMPs), not the AKS itself.

options.a: Keeping records until the claim is paid and the patient balance closed
options.b: Keeping records for 1 year after the date of service under HIPAA
options.c: Maintaining records supporting services billed per payer/regulatory periods
options.d: Transferring records to the patient so the practice need not retain any copies

distractorExplanations.a: Payers and auditors can review claims for years after payment, so records must outlast the closed balance.
distractorExplanations.b: No rule sets a one-year limit; HIPAA requires six years for compliance documentation and payers set multi-year periods.
distractorExplanations.d: The provider must retain its own records to support billed services; giving the patient a copy does not satisfy this.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Retention policies follow CMS/state/false claims standards typically multi-year. These periods are often 5-7 or more years, and longer for some programs.

options.a: Provider fraud cases referred for criminal prosecution by the Department of Justice
options.b: Medicaid eligibility errors in state enrollment determinations
options.c: HIPAA privacy complaints filed by patients against providers
options.d: Medicare improper payments through review of claims and medical necessity

distractorExplanations.a: RACs identify improper payments for recovery; fraud referrals go through UPICs and the OIG, not RAC audits.
distractorExplanations.b: Medicaid eligibility error reviews fall under PERM and state programs, not Medicare RAC audits.
distractorExplanations.c: HIPAA privacy complaints are investigated by HHS Office for Civil Rights, not Recovery Audit Contractors.

options.a: PCI-DSS security and patient authorization/disclosure policies
options.b: HIPAA Security Rule standards that replace PCI-DSS for patients
options.c: PCI-DSS rules permitting CVV storage when the file is encrypted
options.d: Verbal patient consent recorded once at the first visit

distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA does not replace PCI-DSS; card data handled by a medical practice must still meet PCI-DSS.
distractorExplanations.c: PCI-DSS prohibits storing the CVV after authorization, even in encrypted form.
distractorExplanations.d: Card-on-file use needs written authorization with clear terms, not a one-time verbal consent.

options.a: Pay the ransom promptly so systems come back before any patient data is accessed
options.b: Isolate systems, notify leadership/IT, assess breach notification obligations
options.c: Restore from backups and resume billing without a breach assessment
options.d: Notify all patients within 24 hours before the scope is investigated

distractorExplanations.a: Paying does not guarantee recovery or remove breach duties, and may raise sanctions concerns; containment comes first.
distractorExplanations.c: HHS presumes ransomware encryption of PHI is a breach unless a risk assessment shows low probability of compromise.
distractorExplanations.d: HIPAA requires notice without unreasonable delay and within 60 days of discovery, after the scope is assessed.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Cyber incidents require containment, forensic analysis, and potential HIPAA breach notification. Systems are then restored from clean backups.

options.a: Acceptable if each test was medically necessary and performed
options.b: A coding error only if the payer does not catch it
options.c: Fraud/abuse if panels should be billed as panel per policy
options.d: Acceptable when the payer's system pays the claim as billed

distractorExplanations.a: Medical necessity of each test does not permit splitting a panel to get higher payment.
distractorExplanations.b: Intentional unbundling is fraud or abuse whether or not the payer's edits catch it.
distractorExplanations.d: Payment does not make an improper claim proper; overpayments from unbundling must be returned.

options.a: Reporting HIPAA breaches directly to the OCR on staff's behalf
options.b: Answering billing questions from patients about their bills
options.c: Filing appeals of claim denials with payers
options.d: Anonymous/good-faith reporting of suspected violations

distractorExplanations.a: A compliance hotline is an internal reporting channel; it does not file reports with OCR for staff.
distractorExplanations.b: Patient billing questions go to customer service, not the compliance hotline.
distractorExplanations.c: Denial appeals are a revenue cycle task, not the purpose of a compliance hotline.

options.a: Cannot participate in federal healthcare programs
options.b: Can work in billing roles that do not touch patient care
options.c: Is barred from Medicare but may still bill Medicaid
options.d: Regains eligibility once the exclusion is listed for 5 years

distractorExplanations.b: Exclusion covers administrative and management services paid by federal programs, not just patient care.
distractorExplanations.c: OIG exclusion applies to all federal health care programs, including Medicaid.
distractorExplanations.d: Reinstatement requires applying to OIG after the exclusion term; it does not happen at a set listing date.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: LEIE lists individuals/entities excluded from Medicare/Medicaid participation. Hiring them or billing for their services is prohibited.

options.a: In-network deductibles and copays at in-network hospitals
options.b: Out-of-network cost sharing in certain emergency and facility settings
options.c: Out-of-network charges for all elective care chosen by the patient
options.d: Ground ambulance charges from out-of-network providers

distractorExplanations.a: In-network cost sharing is set by the plan; the No Surprises Act targets out-of-network surprise bills.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients can knowingly choose out-of-network elective care after notice and consent; the Act targets surprise bills.
distractorExplanations.d: Ground ambulance is excluded from the No Surprises Act; only air ambulance is covered.

options.a: Attendance only, since topic content is set by CMS
options.b: Topics covered, without tracking individual attendance
options.c: Test scores, used to set staff billing productivity pay
options.d: Attendance, topics covered, and periodic updates

distractorExplanations.a: Topics must be documented too, and CMS does not dictate each practice's training content.
distractorExplanations.b: Auditors expect proof of who attended; topics without attendance records do not show training was completed.
distractorExplanations.c: Tying training to billing productivity pay creates a compliance risk; attendance and topics are what is documented.

medical-billing-specialist-readiness-che.explanation: Documented training demonstrates compliance program effectiveness to auditors. Topics include fraud, waste, abuse, and HIPAA.
